doc.title: John Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 18, 2023 [interview 2 of 2]

chapter: Original songs and the record business
title: Streaming, Spotify and the cost of making a record
summary: He argues that musicians should not give music to Spotify, noting that a good record costs thousands of dollars to make.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: How is the technology of the day affecting selling your music? You made a crack about you had the “Stage & Screen” CD with you at the concert and you found a funny way to put it, you said, “Yeah if you buy the CD next time I come back I’ll sell you a CD player.”

Yeah. I think the thing, my goal, which will never happen but my feeling is I don’t understand why we give all of our music to Spotify. Because that is — I mean there’s this idea that our music is free and there’s no blood, sweat or tears involved in it and money spent on it. I mean there’s a lot of money that’s spent on making a record. It costs just at the cheapest — at the cheapest it’s five thousand dollars I think. I mean to make a good record. And that’s pulling a lot of strings, if you’ll pardon the expression, that’s no pun intended. But I mean a really good record, with horns and everything, you can make, if you’re lucky enough for fifteen thousand dollars and then to twenty. And then we put it on Spotify and let everybody listen to it like, “Oh I listen on Spotify” well I haven’t figured out why we do that. And I keep thinking if we just all said, “You know, we’re going to take a month off and pull all of our music off of Spotify and make people buy our music. It’s only nine dollars for a record, is it twelve dollars? It’s nothing. It’s two beers. It’s one beer somewhere.
Wherever you go, yeah. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

At the Carlyle it’s half a beer. So I think, just that’s the one thing I can’t figure out. And you know luckily my fans like to have the record on them. I don’t have one here. Oh here, “James Taylor.”
